posts.title: AI agents are arriving everywhere, and landing on the cancel list
posts.summary: Gartner expects agents in 40% of enterprise apps by the end of 2026 and predicts over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by 2027. Both can be true.
body: Gartner expects up to 40% of enterprise applications to include task-specific AI agents by the end of 2026, up from under 5% in 2025. The same firm predicts that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, citing rising costs, unclear business value and weak risk controls.

Both forecasts can be true at once. Agents are showing up inside the software teams already use, while many custom agent projects started on hype will stall. Gartner also warns about "agent washing": by its estimate, only about 130 of the thousands of vendors marketing agentic AI offer real agentic capabilities.

From a delivery seat, the pattern is familiar. The projects that survive pick a narrow task with a measured baseline, budget for evaluation and guardrails from day one, and name who approves what the agent does. Projects that start with "let's add an agent" and no success metric are the ones that end up cut.
My takeaway: before funding an agent, write down the decision it supports, the metric it should move, and the control that stops it when it is wrong.

posts.title: AI agents are getting authority faster than they are getting oversight
posts.summary: New surveys show agents approving transactions and changing controls while only 9% of firms have redesigned workflows and 5% of automakers report mature AI governance.
body: Optro surveyed 417 governance, risk, compliance, audit and security leaders at organizations with 250 or more employees in North America and Europe. 38% let AI agents approve or reject transactions, 34% let them modify controls or policies, and 27% let them change user permissions or access rights. Meanwhile, 34% have acted on an inaccurate agent decision or output, 30% have seen an agent take an unintended action, and only 9% have redesigned workflows to accommodate agents.

A Capgemini Research Institute survey of 800 automotive executives shows the same gap in one industry. 68% already use (33%) or pilot (35%) agentic AI in product development, but only 5% report fully mature AI governance. Trust reaches 59% for upstream research and concept work and falls to 40% in development activities.

From a delivery seat, adoption is no longer the bottleneck; oversight is. Optro also found 46% of organizations say employees now spend more time reviewing, validating or correcting AI outputs. That is the hidden cost of dropping an agent into an old workflow instead of redesigning the workflow around it. I treat agent permissions the way I treat privileged access: scoped, logged and reviewed on a schedule.
My takeaway: before an agent can approve, change or grant anything, give that authority a named human owner, an audit trail and a rollback path. If you cannot, keep the agent in recommend-only mode.

posts.title: AI agents need an ID badge and a manager
posts.summary: ServiceNow's AI Passport gives agents a signed runtime credential, and one CISO says every one of his 1,500 agents has an employee ID and a manager.
body: On October 15, ServiceNow announced AI Passport, a cryptographically signed credential that AI agents check at runtime to verify the scope an enterprise has authorized. It applies to ServiceNow and third-party agents and to MCP servers, and it can redirect, restrict or terminate an agent that drifts. It ships with shadow AI detection and 400+ discovery connectors, and is expected in Q4 2026.

The announcement included two numbers worth noting. ServiceNow's 2026 Banking AI Maturity Index found that 100 percent of banks report using AI, but only 24 percent have the governance to match it. And the CISO of LTM said the company has deployed 1,500 AI agents, each assigned an employee ID and manager.

From a delivery seat, that second detail matters more than the product. Once you have dozens of agents across teams and vendors, the hard question is no longer what an agent can do. It is which agent did it, under whose authority, and who answers for it. Identity is how you get there, and it is far easier to design in at the pilot than to retrofit after go-live.
My takeaway: register every agent like a new hire before it touches production. Give it a unique identity, a named human manager, a defined scope and an offboarding date.

posts.title: AI agents are going to work at city hall. Give each one an owner.
posts.summary: State and local pilots show real gains from AI agents, and the Urban Institute's playbook says governance has to come first, with seven named roles per agent.
body: State and local governments are moving past chatbots. As PYMNTS reported on October 19, a Virginia pilot used agentic AI to review regulatory documents, identifying more than $1.4 billion in annual savings and cutting permit and license processing times by nearly 80 percent. In Utah, a prescription renewal pilot recommended renewal in 72 percent of cases, and physicians agreed with 91 percent of those recommendations. A World Economic Forum framework cited in the same piece maps 70 government functions and finds half are ready for agentic AI.

The Urban Institute's Responsible Agentic AI Playbook explains why results like these need structure behind them. Agents can be built by staff outside IT, which speeds things up but raises the risk of errors, especially in areas like benefits. The playbook asks agencies to document each agent's purpose, target population, outcomes and costs, and to scale oversight to how public-facing the agent is.

From a delivery seat, the most useful part is the roles. The playbook names seven: accountable owner, evaluation lead, security lead, transparency lead, responsible AI lead, contributor and independent review. That turns governance from a policy memo into a staffing plan you can actually check.
My takeaway: before an agent goes live, fill in those seven names. If a seat is empty, the agent is not ready.

posts.title: The AI agent value gap is a stop-rule gap
posts.summary: Gartner's new surveys show only 13% of CIOs see significant AI value. The leaders have rules for killing pilots and plans to redesign roles around agents.
body: This week at Gartner IT Symposium, the numbers on AI value were sobering. A survey of 2,002 CIOs and technology executives found only 13% say their enterprise has realized significant or transformational value from AI, and use case success is still about one in five. A separate CEO survey found 44% of CEOs struggle to show AI financial returns, yet 52% named aggressively deploying AI agents as employees as a top move to get there. Meanwhile, 71% of organizations expect to deploy agentic AI within 12 months, while only 21% have agentic AI governance in place.

What separates the leaders is discipline, not spend. Organizations with rules for stopping a pilot before production are 2.3 times more likely to be what Gartner calls vanguards, and those with rules for retiring low-value AI already in production are 2.6 times more likely. Only 31% and 17% of CIOs have those rules. Just 4% have plans to redesign roles for a human-agent workforce, a practice tied to 2.4 times better odds.

From a delivery seat, this matches what I see in portfolios: agents are easy to start and hard to stop. Without exit criteria, pilots linger, costs grow, and no one owns the decision to shut them down.
My takeaway: write the kill criteria into every agent charter before the first sprint, and review them at the production gate and quarterly after.

posts.title: Human review is back in the AI agent plan. Budget for it.
posts.summary: Fewer enterprises now let AI agents ship production changes without a human check, even as many report agents that passed testing and still failed in front of customers.
body: Enterprises are pulling back on letting AI agents act unchecked. In VentureBeat Intelligence's August survey, 56% of organizations deploying autonomous agents allow, or are building toward, production changes based on automated evaluations alone, down from 75% in July. The share planning to keep human review for the foreseeable future rose from 20% to 42%. Meanwhile, 61% of respondents running pre-deployment evaluations reported an agent or LLM feature that passed internal testing and then caused a customer-facing failure within 12 months.

IBM's new survey of 3,221 executives across Europe and the Middle East shows the same tension. 35% run agentic AI in production and 75% expect agents to have some decision autonomy by 2027, yet only 37% say their governance is designed to scale with agentic AI. What they say they will need: defined human escalation thresholds (32%), real-time monitoring and audit trails (30%), and the ability to halt agent activity immediately (29%).

From a delivery seat, this is a healthy correction, not a retreat. Passing a test suite is not the same as being right in production, and only 29% of agent deployers primarily use real-time quality checks on live outputs. Human review is a real workload, and it needs capacity, owners and a plan to shrink it as evidence builds.
My takeaway: put reviewer hours and an escalation path in the agent's delivery plan, and define the production evidence that lets you reduce review over time.
